Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Omar Khalil, a 37-year-old married firefighter from a Middle Eastern family, came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed around one terrifying period in which he had been stalked. The stalking had begun with small, unsettling details he could not dismiss: a bicycle left repeatedly outside his station and later near his home, a shadowy figure seeming to appear at the edge of streets he used on his commute, and the sickening sense that he was being followed or tracked even when he tried to tell himself he was overreacting. What made the experience especially potent was that it invaded the ordinary spaces of his day—driving to work, walking into a building, stepping outside after a shift—so that physical locations no longer felt neutral. During the most frightening stretches, Omar would enter a room and immediately scan for exits, and he became intensely alert to unexpected or loud sounds, because each abrupt noise felt to him like the start of something he had to prepare for.

As the stalking continued, those triggers began pulling the event back into him with little warning. Seeing a bicycle locked near the firehouse, passing a familiar intersection, or noticing a car pacing him on the road could instantly bring the full memory back, not as a distant recollection but as a rush that made him stop what he was doing. He described how the memory would arrive in pieces he could not hold onto for long: he knew what had happened, yet when he tried to explain it he found himself unable to find the words, and the emotion rose so quickly that he had to break off and sit in silence. Each return of the memory seemed to confirm what he had already started to believe about himself. Omar had come to think that he had permanently changed for the worse, that the fear and jumpiness meant he was going crazy, and that his inability to handle the situation showed he was weak in a way he had never allowed himself to be before. The more the memory broke through, the more it fed those beliefs, and the more ashamed and altered he felt.

Those appraisals quickly spread into the way he moved through the world. Believing that he had been weakened and was no longer trustworthy in his own judgment, Omar became even more on guard. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, especially when he was off duty or alone, and the moment he entered any room or building his eyes went to doors, hallways, and exits. Because he was convinced that danger could appear without warning and that he was no longer the man he had been, he began treating ordinary places as if they were potential traps. A quiet restaurant, the grocery store, the parking lot outside his station, even the gym near his home all became settings where he felt the need to check who was behind him and whether someone might be tracking his route. He avoided certain streets and found himself making detours that lengthened his commute, and after a while the bicycle itself—once merely a detail in the stalking—became enough to set his whole body on edge.

What frightened Omar most was how the threat state seemed to keep his mind tied to the event. An unexpected bang in the station, a slammed locker door, or footsteps too close behind him would send him back to the same conviction that he was under watch and had to stay ready. That vigilance, in turn, made him think even more harshly about himself: if he had to keep scanning, if he could never relax, then something in him must be fundamentally damaged. On the worst days, the memory would surface while he was already alert, and the combination left him feeling overwhelmed and exposed, as though he were failing at the very job that depended on steadiness. Over weeks and months, this fed a tightening cycle in which every sign of being followed or every sharp sound confirmed his fear, and every confirmation deepened his sense of permanent change and weakness. He withdrew from colleagues, stopped lingering after shifts, and became wary even in the company of other people because he could not shake the sense that someone might mean him harm.

By the time he sought help, Omar was exhausted by living this way and frightened by how small his world had become. He said he wanted to keep protecting his family and doing his work, but he was most afraid that if he continued alone he would either break down completely or remain trapped in this state of watching, checking, and reliving.
